section.title: Moses Flees to Midian
section.sectionRationale: The seam falls at the time jump of verse 11, after grown, then closes at the death of the king and God's remembering His covenant in verse 25, just before the burning bush. Three scenes carry it: Moses' violent intervention and flight, his rescue of Jethro's daughters, and the groaning of Israel reaching God.
section.thesis: Moses' own attempt to deliver his people by force fails and exiles him for forty years, but even in exile God is quietly forming a shepherd, and He has not forgotten the cries of His people.
section.frameNote: Three scenes: Moses kills an Egyptian and flees; he rescues Reuel's daughters and settles in Midian; Israel's groaning under bondage reaches God, who remembers His covenant.

units.label: A premature deliverance
units.note: Moses takes matters into his own hands

verses.text: One day, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his own people and observed their hard labor. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own people.
After looking this way and that and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid his body in the sand.
The next day Moses went out and saw two Hebrews fighting. He asked the one in the wrong, “Why are you attacking your companion?”

But the man replied, “Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you planning to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?” Then Moses was afraid and thought, “This thing I have done has surely become known.”
When Pharaoh heard about this matter, he sought to kill Moses. But Moses fled from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian, where he sat down beside a well.
Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came to draw water and fill the troughs to water their father's flock.
And when some shepherds came along and drove them away, Moses rose up to help them and watered their flock.
When the daughters returned to their father Reuel, he asked them, “Why have you returned so early today?”
“An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds,” they replied. “He even drew water for us and watered the flock.”
“So where is he?” their father asked. “Why did you leave the man behind? Invite him to have something to eat.”
Moses agreed to stay with the man, and he gave his daughter Zipporah to Moses in marriage.
And she gave birth to a son, and Moses named him {{gershom|Gershom}}, saying, “I have become a foreigner in a foreign land.”
After a long time, the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned and {{zaaq|cried out}} under their burden of slavery, and their cry for deliverance from bondage ascended to God.
So God heard their groaning, and He {{zakar|remembered}} His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
God saw the Israelites and took notice.

gershom.gloss: Sounds like the Hebrew for foreigner, ger. Moses names his son for his own experience: rescued from Egypt only to become a stranger in Midian, a man without a settled home, being shaped in exile for a mission he does not yet see.

zaaq.gloss: To cry out in distress, often the cry of the oppressed for justice. This is the cry that reaches God's ears throughout Scripture and moves Him to act on behalf of the powerless.

zakar.gloss: To remember. Not forgetting after a lapse, but bringing a prior commitment into active effect. God remembering His covenant means He is about to act on the promise He made to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

basic.context: Moses, now grown, sees his people's suffering and tries to fix it his own way, killing an Egyptian in anger. It backfires, and he flees for his life to Midian, where he becomes a shepherd, marries, and has a son. Meanwhile back in Egypt, the king dies, but the suffering continues, and the Israelites cry out to God, who remembers His promise.
basic.hermeneutics: This is real history describing Moses' failed attempt at self-made deliverance and God's patient timing. The passage does not teach that anger or vigilante violence is the way to serve God; it shows what happens when a person tries to act ahead of God's timing and calling.
basic.originalLanguages: Moses names his son Gershom, sounding like ger, foreigner, since he has become a stranger in a strange land. And Israel's cry, tsaaq, reaches God, who then zakar, remembers, His covenant, bringing His ancient promise into active motion.
basic.typology: Moses' rejected first attempt to deliver his people, followed by exile and a second, God-appointed call, foreshadows how Israel first rejected her true deliverer at His first coming before receiving Him fully at His return, and how every true deliverance must come from God's initiative, not human striving.
basic.christ: Moses' zeal that misfires here contrasts with Christ's perfect, patient obedience to the Father's timing; where Moses strikes in anger and must flee, Jesus lays down His life in willing submission at exactly the appointed hour, John 7:6.
basic.god: God appears to be silent for forty years, yet He is never absent; He is shaping Moses in obscurity and hears every groan of His oppressed people. When the moment is right, the text says plainly that He remembered His covenant, an assurance that His promises do not expire.
basic.crossReferences: Acts 7:23-29 retells this scene in Stephen's speech, noting Moses supposed his brothers would understand God was giving them deliverance through him. Genesis 15:13-14 predicted this exact bondage and its end. Psalm 105:8 celebrates God remembering His covenant forever.
basic.oneStory: This is the long, hidden middle of the story: a failed rescue, decades of obscurity, and a cry that does not go unheard. It teaches that God's deliverance comes on His timetable, not ours, and it points forward to the true and better Deliverer who came at exactly the right time, Galatians 4:4.

context.literary:
Exodus 2:11-25 falls into three scenes, and each ends with Moses or Israel in a new place. In verses 11 to 15 Moses goes out, sees, strikes and flees. In verses 16 to 22 he sits by a well, rises, rescues and settles. In verses 23 to 25 the camera pulls away from Moses altogether and fixes on God. The movement is from a man acting on his own sight to God acting on His.

The first two scenes are built as a matched pair. Each has an oppressor (the Egyptian, the shepherds), a victim (a Hebrew labourer, seven daughters) and an intervention by Moses. The first ends in bloodshed, rejection and flight; the second ends in hospitality, marriage and a son. The same instinct for justice produces opposite results, and the difference is not Moses' strength but where he is standing.

The scene at the well also borrows a familiar pattern from Genesis. Abraham's servant meets Rebekah at a well, Genesis 24:11-20, and Jacob meets Rachel at one, Genesis 29:1-12. In each case a traveller from far away arrives, water is drawn, the girls run home, hospitality follows and a marriage is arranged. Moses steps into the story of the patriarchs. The fugitive is being folded back into the family line of promise.

The closing paragraph, verses 23 to 25, is a hinge for the whole book. After two chapters in which God is almost silent, He is suddenly the subject of four verbs in a row: He heard, He remembered, He saw, He knew. The paragraph looks back to Exodus 1 and forward to the bush of chapter 3, where God will repeat these very verbs to Moses, Exodus 3:7-9.
context.historical:
Stephen says Moses was forty years old when he went out to his brothers, Acts 7:23, and Exodus 7:7 makes him eighty when he stood before Pharaoh. Stephen's figure of forty years in Midian, Acts 7:30, fits that span. Moses had been raised in the royal household, Exodus 2:10, and would have known the court from the inside. A killing by a man of that standing was not a private matter, which is why Pharaoh himself hears of it and seeks his death, verse 15.

Midian lay outside Egypt's direct control, generally placed east of the Gulf of Aqaba, though its tribes ranged widely through the Sinai and the desert fringes. The Midianites traced their line to Abraham through Keturah, Genesis 25:1-2, so Moses finds refuge among distant kin. His father-in-law is a priest, and the text uses two names for him: Reuel here, verse 18, and Jethro in Exodus 3:1 and 18:1. Numbers 10:29 speaks of Hobab son of Reuel, and Judges 1:16 calls the family Kenites. Clans often carried more than one name, and the Bible does not stop to harmonise them.

Wells were the social centre of pastoral life. Access to water could be contested, and the strong shepherds pushing the women aside, verse 17, reflects a real and daily injustice. A stranger who defended a household's women and flock placed that household in his debt, and Reuel's rebuke of his daughters for failing to invite him, verse 20, reflects the heavy duty of hospitality in the ancient Near East.

The death of the king of Egypt, verse 23, marks a change of reign, but not a change of policy. Scholars who date the exodus early, from 1 Kings 6:1, often identify him with a king of the fifteenth century BC; those who date it later, from the store city named Rameses in Exodus 1:11, look to the thirteenth. The text never names him, which is itself a statement: the kings pass, but the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob remains.
context.canonical:
Genesis had already announced this chapter. God told Abram his descendants would be strangers in a land not their own, enslaved and mistreated four hundred years, and that He would judge the nation they served, Genesis 15:13-14. Exodus 2:24 is the moment that word begins to move, and Exodus 6:5 repeats it almost verbatim: 'I have heard the groaning of the Israelites... and I have remembered My covenant.'

The pattern of verse 23 to 25, affliction, a cry, God hearing and raising a deliverer, becomes the rhythm of Israel's history. Deuteronomy 26:7 turns it into a confession Israel recited at the firstfruits: 'the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction, toil, and oppression.' Judges repeats it cycle after cycle, 'when the Israelites cried out to the LORD, He raised up... a deliverer,' Judges 3:9, and says God 'was moved to pity by their groaning,' Judges 2:18. The psalms celebrate the same memory, Psalm 105:42 and Psalm 106:44-45, and Leviticus 26:42 promises that even after exile God will remember His covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham.

The New Testament reads this chapter twice. Stephen retells it in Acts 7:23-29 and draws out what Exodus leaves implicit: Moses 'assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him to deliver them, but they did not,' Acts 7:25. He then makes the rejected ruler a pattern for Israel's rejection of Jesus, Acts 7:35 and 7:51-52. Hebrews reads Moses' choice as faith, 'He chose to suffer oppression with God's people,' Hebrews 11:25. Zechariah's song in Luke 1:72 praises God for coming 'to remember His holy covenant,' the same remembering that opens the exodus now opening a greater one.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses, writing of himself, does not flatter his younger self. He wants Israel to see that the deliverance they later enjoyed did not begin with a gifted man seizing the moment. The one who would lead them out first tried to do it with his own hands, in secret, looking 'this way and that,' verse 12, and it came to nothing. His own people rejected him, and he ran.

The author also wants Israel to see that failure was not the end of God's purpose for Moses. The same impulse to defend the weak reappears at the well, and this time it serves. The prince becomes a shepherd, the courtier becomes a foreigner, and the man who acted alone learns to wait. Israel, who would spend forty years of their own in the wilderness, were meant to recognise that God does His deepest shaping in obscure places.

Most of all, the author wants Israel to know that their cry was heard before any deliverer appeared. The chapter closes with God, not Moses. The first hearers, remembering their own groaning, were meant to trust that the covenant God remembers, sees and knows, and to cry out to Him rather than despair.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage records a killing, a concealment, a flight and a marriage outside Israel. None of these is presented as a model. The text is careful: Moses checks that no one is watching, hides the body, and is afraid when it becomes known, verses 12 and 14. Those details do not commend the act, and Stephen's comment that his brothers 'did not' understand, Acts 7:25, shows that his timing was his own.

What does carry forward is more indirect. Moses' refusal to stand by while the weak were beaten, both in Egypt and at the well, is consistent with the law he would later give: Israel must not oppress the foreigner, widow or orphan, for God hears their cry, Exodus 22:21-23. The concern for justice is right; the lone and hidden violence is not. The closing verses give a prescription by implication: those who suffer under oppression may bring their groaning to God, who hears it. And those who know they are foreigners, as Moses named his son, are invited to live as the patriarchs did, as strangers who trust God's promise, Hebrews 11:13 and 1 Peter 2:11.

debates.question: Was Moses right or wrong to kill the Egyptian?

views.label: A sinful, premature act
views.case: Moses acts secretly, verse 12, without any word from God, and is afraid once it is known, verse 14. Nothing in Exodus commends the act, and Moses' later calling comes only after forty years away. On this reading the killing is a manslaughter born of anger, and the flight is its fruit.

views.label: A flawed but zealous act of faith
views.case: Hebrews 11:24-26 says Moses chose to suffer with God's people and valued disgrace for Christ above Egypt's treasures. Stephen says Moses 'went to his defense and avenged him,' Acts 7:24, and assumed God was using him to deliver them, Acts 7:25. The motive was loyalty to God's people, even though the method and timing were wrong.

debates.bearing: Most interpreters hold both together: Moses' concern for his people was right, but his method and timing were not God's, and the episode teaches that even good ends do not justify taking matters into our own hands ahead of God.

debates.question: Does Hebrews 11:27, 'By faith Moses left Egypt, not fearing the king's anger,' refer to this flight to Midian?

views.label: Yes, the flight to Midian
views.case: Hebrews moves in order through Moses' life, and verse 27 comes after his choice to identify with Israel, verses 24 to 26, and before the Passover, verse 28. On this reading Moses' flight was not cowardice at heart but a refusal to return to Pharaoh's favour, persevering because he saw Him who is invisible.

views.label: No, the exodus itself
views.case: Exodus 2:14 says plainly that Moses was afraid, which seems hard to square with 'not fearing the king's anger.' At the exodus Moses left Egypt openly, defying Pharaoh's fury, Exodus 10:28-29. Some read Hebrews 11:27 as looking ahead to that departure, with verse 28 then stepping back to the Passover night that made it possible.

debates.bearing: Either reading leaves the Exodus account honest: Moses was afraid when his deed became known. Hebrews does not deny that fear; it looks past it to the faith that kept Moses from ever going back to Egypt's treasures. The Bible can record a believer's fear and still call his life faith.

study.originalLanguages:
The first scene turns on one verb used three times. The Egyptian was 'beating' a Hebrew, verse 11; Moses 'struck down' the Egyptian, verse 12; and the next day Moses asks the Hebrew, 'Why are you attacking your companion?' verse 13. All three are forms of nakah, to strike. English uses three verbs, but the Hebrew makes the reader feel the cycle: blow answers blow, and violence among the oppressed mirrors violence against them. The same verb returns when God promises to 'strike the Egyptians with all the wonders,' Exodus 3:20. The striking that Moses tried to do by his own hand will be done by God's.

The man Moses rebukes is called 'the one in the wrong,' verse 13, a single word in Hebrew, rasha, the ordinary word for the wicked or guilty party in a dispute, as in the law's instruction to condemn 'the guilty' in court, Deuteronomy 25:1. His retort, 'Who made you ruler and judge over us?' verse 14, pairs sar, a prince or official, with shophet, a judge. Moses was in fact a prince of Egypt. The man is asking by what right a prince of Pharaoh presumes to judge Hebrews. Stephen quotes the line twice, Acts 7:27 and 7:35, and the BSB footnote notes that the Greek adds 'yesterday,' which Acts 7:28 follows.

The verb yashab, to sit or settle, frames the next scene. Moses 'settled' in the land of Midian and 'sat down' beside a well, verse 15, both yashab; he 'agreed to stay' with Reuel, verse 21, again yashab. The man who could not stay in Egypt comes to rest. In contrast, the daughters say an Egyptian 'rescued' them, verse 19, using natsal, the verb God uses in Exodus 3:8, 'I have come down to rescue them.' The narrator himself says Moses 'rose up to help them,' verse 17, with yasha, to save, the verb of Exodus 14:30, 'the LORD saved Israel,' and the root of the names Joshua and Jesus.

Gershom, verse 22, sounds like ger, a resident foreigner, as the BSB footnote says. The ger was a person living on land that was not his own, without the protection of kin. Abraham called himself one at Hebron, Genesis 23:4, and the law made Israel's own years as foreigners in Egypt the reason to protect the foreigner among them, Exodus 22:21. Moses gives the word to his firstborn, marking him as heir of Abraham's condition.

The closing verses pile up words for distress. Israel 'groaned,' anach, 'cried out,' zaaq, and their 'cry for deliverance,' shawah, rose to God; God heard their 'groaning,' neaqah, verse 24, the same word He uses when He repeats this moment in Exodus 6:5. God is the subject of the last four verbs: heard, remembered, saw and, literally, 'knew,' verse 25. The Hebrew sentence stops there, with no object. The BSB renders it 'took notice.' The Greek translators read the consonants a little differently and made it 'He made Himself known to them,' which is exactly what the next chapter narrates.

typology.type: The deliverer rejected by his own, Exodus 2:14
typology.fulfillment: Stephen makes this the key to the whole story: 'This Moses, whom they had rejected with the words, Who made you ruler and judge? is the one whom God sent to be their ruler and redeemer,' Acts 7:35. Jesus came to His own, and His own did not receive Him, John 1:11; He was handed over and rejected, Acts 3:13-14, and God exalted Him 'as Prince and Savior,' Acts 5:31. The escalation is that Moses was rejected for a real wrong, while Jesus was rejected as 'the Holy and Righteous One,' Acts 3:14. Moses' rejection exposed his haste; Christ's exposed the hearts of those who refused Him.

typology.type: The prince who becomes a shepherd, Exodus 2:16-21
typology.fulfillment: Moses leaves a palace for the pasture and learns to water another man's flock, the training ground for leading Israel 'like a flock,' Psalm 77:20 and Isaiah 63:11. Jesus left far greater glory and emptied Himself, 'taking the form of a servant,' Philippians 2:7, and He calls Himself the good shepherd who 'lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11. The type falls short at the decisive point: Moses fled to save his own life, while the good shepherd walked toward death to save His flock. Moses guarded sheep that belonged to Jethro; Christ lays down His life for sheep He calls His own.

typology.type: The stranger who sits down beside a well, Exodus 2:15
typology.fulfillment: Like Jacob before him, Moses meets his bride at a well. John tells of Jesus, weary from His journey, who 'sat down by the well' at Sychar, John 4:6, and there offers a Samaritan woman living water. The setting borrows the betrothal scene of the patriarchs, and John 3:29 has already called Jesus the bridegroom. The escalation is striking: Moses draws water for a flock and wins a wife, while Christ gives water that becomes 'a fount of water springing up to eternal life,' John 4:14, and gathers a people to Himself. The echo is John's, carried by the setting, not a stated type.

typology.type: The groaning that rises to God, Exodus 2:23-24
typology.fulfillment: Israel's groaning under slavery reaches God, and He moves to redeem. Paul hears the same sound on a wider scale: 'the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth,' and believers too 'groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies,' Romans 8:22-23. The Spirit Himself intercedes 'with groans too deep for words,' Romans 8:26. The escalation is that God does not only hear the groaning from above; in the Spirit He takes it up from within His people. The exodus freed one nation from one Pharaoh; the redemption Paul awaits frees the whole creation from its bondage to decay.

study.christ:
The strongest link between this passage and Christ is drawn by the New Testament itself. Stephen's speech in Acts 7 is built on a pattern: God sends a deliverer, His people fail to understand, they push him away, and God vindicates him anyway. Joseph, Acts 7:9-10, and Moses, Acts 7:25-35, both follow it, and Stephen concludes by charging his hearers with killing 'the Righteous One,' Acts 7:52. The words of the Hebrew in Exodus 2:14, 'Who made you ruler and judge over us?' become the voice of every generation that refuses the one God sends.

The contrast is as instructive as the likeness. Moses tried to establish justice with a hidden blow. When a man asked Jesus to settle an inheritance, He replied, 'Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?' Luke 12:14, almost the question put to Moses, but now on the lips of the true Judge declining to rule before His hour. When Peter drew a sword in the garden, Jesus told him to put it away, since He could call on more than twelve legions of angels, Matthew 26:52-53, and He told Pilate, 'My kingdom is not of this world; if it were, My servants would fight,' John 18:36. The deliverer Moses was not yet, Jesus was fully: He wins not by striking the oppressor in secret but by being struck in public.

The passage also leads to Christ through the theme of the foreigner. Moses names his son for his homelessness, and Jesus says 'the Son of Man has no place to lay His head,' Matthew 8:20. He became a stranger so that strangers might be brought home. Hebrews 11:26 even says Moses 'valued disgrace for Christ above the treasures of Egypt.' The writer does not mean Moses knew the name of Jesus, but that the reproach Moses bore by siding with God's people was the same kind of reproach the Messiah would bear, and it was worth more than a palace.

Finally, the four verbs of verses 24 and 25 find their fullest answer in the Son. Hebrews says that Jesus 'offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard,' Hebrews 5:7. The God who heard Israel's groaning heard His Son's cry, and raised Him. Zechariah blesses God because in the coming of Jesus He has acted 'to remember His holy covenant,' Luke 1:72. The covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob that God remembered in Egypt is the covenant He kept in Christ.

Care is needed here. Moses' killing of the Egyptian is not a picture of the cross, and the seven daughters and the troughs are not symbols of anything. The links rest on the New Testament's own reading of Moses as a rejected ruler and on the covenant thread that runs from Exodus 2:24 to Luke 1:72.
study.god:
This passage teaches something about God by His near absence. For most of Exodus 1 and 2 He is scarcely named as acting. The midwives fear Him, and He deals well with them, Exodus 1:17-21, but otherwise the story is told in terms of kings, labour, a basket and a princess. Then in three verses the narrator names Him five times. The reader is meant to feel that God was never absent from the story, only unannounced. Providence works under the surface of ordinary events, the timing of a princess's bath, a quarrel between labourers, a well in Midian, until the moment God chooses to be seen acting.

God's remembering is covenantal, not psychological. When Scripture says God remembered Noah, Genesis 8:1, or Rachel, Genesis 30:22, or Hannah, 1 Samuel 1:19, it is followed at once by action: the waters subside, the womb opens, a child is born. 'God remembered His covenant' means God is about to act on His promise. The covenant here is the one with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the text names all three, underlining that the God of Exodus is the same God who spoke in Genesis 15:13-14 of this very bondage.

He is also the God who sees and knows. The verb ra'ah, to see, has run all through the chapter: Pharaoh's daughter saw the basket, Exodus 2:5; Moses saw the Egyptian beating the Hebrew, verse 11; Moses looked this way and that and saw no one, verse 12. Moses looked around to make sure he was unseen. The chapter ends by saying God saw, verse 25. Nothing done in Egypt was hidden from Him, not the violence of the taskmasters, not Moses' secret blow, not Israel's anguish. That is both a comfort and a warning.

The passage holds together God's patience and His compassion. Forty years pass between Moses' flight and his call, and Israel's suffering continues under a new king. Yet the text does not present God as indifferent during that time; it presents Him as preparing both a deliverer and a moment. His timing is not slow in the way people count slowness. The law He later gives shows how seriously He takes the cry of the oppressed: 'If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to Me in distress, I will surely hear their cry,' Exodus 22:23.

For worship, the passage invites the kind of prayer Israel prayed without knowing to whom they prayed. Verse 23 does not say they cried to the LORD, only that their cry 'ascended to God.' Even a groan without words reached Him. Believers may bring grief they cannot shape into sentences, trusting the God who hears, remembers, sees and knows.

crossReferences.note: God tells Abram that his descendants will be strangers in a foreign land, enslaved and mistreated four hundred years, and that He will judge the nation they serve. Exodus 2:24 says God remembered His covenant with Abraham; this is the covenant word being remembered, and Exodus is its unfolding.

Jacob meets Rachel at a well, waters her father's flock and is welcomed into the household. Moses' rescue of Reuel's daughters follows the same betrothal pattern, telling the reader that the exile is being drawn back into the story of the patriarchs even while he lives far from his people.

Stephen retells the scene and adds what Exodus only implies: Moses was forty, he acted as the avenger of his brother, and he assumed they would understand that God was using him to deliver them. They did not. Stephen quotes the Greek form of Exodus 2:14, with 'yesterday' added.

Stephen turns the rejection into a pattern. The Moses whom they rejected as 'ruler and judge' is the one God sent as 'ruler and redeemer.' The words of Exodus 2:14 are answered by God's own appointment, and the pattern prepares Stephen's charge that his hearers have rejected the Righteous One, Acts 7:52.

Hebrews reads Moses' identification with the enslaved as a choice of faith, valuing disgrace for Christ above Egypt's treasures. It gives the inner reason for what Exodus 2:11 describes only outwardly: Moses went out to his own people because he looked ahead to a reward Egypt could not give.

God repeats to Moses almost the words of Exodus 2:24: 'I have heard the groaning of the Israelites... and I have remembered My covenant.' The narrator's report in chapter 2 becomes God's own promise in chapter 6, spoken to a discouraged Moses after Pharaoh has made the burden heavier.

The confession Israel recited when bringing firstfruits into the land preserves this moment in worship: 'we called out to the LORD... and the LORD heard our voice and saw our affliction, toil, and oppression.' Exodus 2:23-25 became part of Israel's creed, recited by every generation.

The pattern of Exodus 2:23-25 becomes the rhythm of the judges: God raised up deliverers because He was 'moved to pity by their groaning under those who oppressed them.' The word groaning links the two passages, and each judge becomes a lesser echo of the deliverer God raised from Midian.

The law turns Israel's memory into ethics. They must not oppress the foreigner, for they were foreigners in Egypt, and if the widow or orphan cries out to God, He will surely hear their cry. The God who heard Israel's cry in Exodus 2 hears every oppressed person's cry in the same way.

Asked to divide an inheritance, Jesus replies, 'Man, who appointed Me judge or executor between you?' The question echoes the challenge thrown at Moses in Exodus 2:14, but now the one asked is the true Judge, who declines to seize a role before the hour the Father has set.

Jesus offered prayers 'with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard.' The God who heard the groaning of Israel in Exodus 2:23-24 heard the cry of His Son, and the answer was resurrection, the deliverance to which the exodus points.

Zechariah praises God for acting 'to show mercy to our fathers and to remember His holy covenant.' The language of Exodus 2:24 is taken up at the dawn of the gospel: the covenant God remembered in Egypt He now remembers in sending the Messiah.

study.oneStory:
Genesis ends with a promise and a coffin. Joseph dies in Egypt, certain that God will come to his family and bring them up to the land, Genesis 50:24-25. Exodus 1 then shows the family multiplying as God had told Adam and Abraham, but that very fruitfulness becomes the reason for their slavery. The blessing of creation is being crushed by a king who fears it. Exodus 2 asks whether God's promises can survive that.

This passage gives the answer in two halves. The first half shows that a human solution cannot deliver God's people. Moses has every advantage, royal learning, strength, and a heart for his brothers, yet his attempt ends in a body in the sand and a fugitive in the desert. This is the same lesson Genesis kept teaching through Abraham's schemes and Jacob's grasping: the promise will be kept by God, not seized by man.

The second half shows that God has not let go. He is preparing Moses as a shepherd in the land of Abraham's other descendants. He hears Israel's groaning, remembers the covenant, sees and knows. Everything that follows, the bush, the plagues, the Passover, the sea and Sinai, flows from those four verbs. The exodus becomes the Old Testament's great picture of redemption, and the prophets later speak of a new exodus when God will bring His people home from exile.

The story finds its centre in Christ. He is the deliverer who was rejected by His own and then exalted, Acts 7:35 and 5:31. He is the Son who became a foreigner with nowhere to lay His head, and He is the one whose cry was heard, Hebrews 5:7. In Him God remembered His holy covenant, Luke 1:72. The redemption He accomplished is an exodus from a slavery deeper than Egypt's: from sin and death.

And the story is not yet finished. The groaning of Exodus 2 has not stopped. Paul says the whole creation groans, and believers groan with it, waiting for the redemption of the body, Romans 8:22-23. The final exodus comes when the creation itself is set free from its bondage, Romans 8:21, and the God who heard, remembered, saw and knew dwells with His people, wiping every tear from their eyes, Revelation 21:3-4. Then no one will be a foreigner any longer, and the cry of the oppressed will be answered for good.

quiz.q: Why did Moses flee to Midian?

options.text: The Israelites banished him themselves.
options.note: It was Pharaoh, not the Israelites, who sought to kill him; a fellow Hebrew merely exposed what he had done.

options.text: He wanted to explore new lands out of curiosity.
options.note: The text gives a specific reason, fear for his life, not curiosity.

options.text: Pharaoh sought to kill him after he killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew.
options.note: Verses 12 and 15 record this act and Pharaoh's response directly.

options.text: He was sent by God on an official mission.
options.note: This was not a commissioned mission; it was flight from Pharaoh's wrath after his own violent act.

quiz.q: What does Acts 7 suggest about Moses' motive in striking the Egyptian?

options.text: He had no connection to his Hebrew identity at this point.
options.note: The text says he went out to his own people, showing he identified with them.

options.text: He supposed his people would understand God was giving them deliverance through him, but the timing and method were his own, not God's.
options.note: Acts 7:25 records this exact reasoning, showing zeal without God's timing or command.

options.text: He was directly commanded by God to kill the Egyptian.
options.note: No divine command is recorded; this was Moses' own initiative.

options.text: He acted purely out of random cruelty.
options.note: Scripture presents his concern for his oppressed people as genuine, even if his method was wrong.

quiz.q: How did Moses come to marry Zipporah?

options.text: Moses never married in Midian.
options.note: The text explicitly records his marriage to Zipporah.

options.text: Pharaoh arranged the marriage as a reward.
options.note: Pharaoh sought to kill Moses; he had no role in this marriage.

options.text: He defended Reuel's daughters from shepherds at a well and was welcomed into their household.
options.note: Verses 16 to 21 describe this sequence of events leading to the marriage.

options.text: Their marriage was arranged before Moses ever fled Egypt.
options.note: The marriage arises from the well encounter after his flight, not from any prior arrangement.

quiz.q: What does the name Gershom mean, and why does Moses choose it?

options.text: It means mighty deliverer.
options.note: The text gives a different, more personal meaning tied to Moses' exile experience.

options.text: It is simply a family name with no meaning.
options.note: The text explicitly explains the name's significance.

options.text: It celebrates Moses' return to Egypt.
options.note: The name reflects exile in Midian, not any return to Egypt, which had not yet happened.

options.text: It echoes the Hebrew word for foreigner, reflecting Moses' experience as a stranger in Midian.
options.note: Verse 22 gives Moses' own explanation, I have become a foreigner in a foreign land.

quiz.q: What four things does the text say God did in response to Israel's groaning at the end of chapter 2?

options.text: He heard their groaning, remembered His covenant, saw the Israelites, and took notice.
options.note: Verses 24 to 25 list exactly these four verbs of divine attention and response.

options.text: He immediately sent plagues on Egypt.
options.note: The plagues come much later; this passage records God's attention and remembering, not yet the plagues.

options.text: Nothing; the text is silent on God's response.
options.note: The text is explicit and emphatic about God's attentive response.

options.text: He forgot about Israel until Moses reminded Him.
options.note: The text says the opposite, that God remembered His covenant on His own initiative.

questions: Moses tried to deliver his people in his own strength and timing, and it backfired. Where might you be trying to force a solution ahead of God's timing rather than waiting on Him?
Moses spent forty hidden years as a shepherd before God called him. What is God quietly forming in you during a season that feels unproductive or overlooked?
Moses named his son for his own experience of being a foreigner. How does it help you to know that even seasons of exile and displacement can be part of God's preparation for a larger purpose?
The text says Israel's groaning reached God, and He remembered His covenant. What burden are you carrying that you need to trust God has not forgotten, even if deliverance feels delayed?
God saw and took notice of His suffering people even during years of apparent silence. Where do you need to trust that God sees you, even when He seems quiet?

translationNotes.note: This verse is cited in Acts 7:27-28 and 7:35, where Stephen applies the crowd's rejection of Moses, Who made you ruler and judge over us, to Israel's later rejection of Jesus.
The priest of Midian is named Reuel here, and Jethro in Exodus 3:1; most understand these as the same man, either two names or a name and a title, since Jethro means his excellency.
Gershom sounds like the Hebrew for foreigner, ger, a name Moses chooses to mark his own experience of exile in Midian.
